opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, a lot of it came down to the people and how they engaged with the problem itself. When you're building something like what we're doing, an AI system that reasons mathematically and can actually verify its own proofs, you need investors who don't just see it as "another LLM company." You need people willing to sit with the technical details and understand why formal verification matters, why math is such a powerful testbed for reasoning, and why this could matter well beyond math.

From our earliest conversations, the Menlo team asked the right questions. They weren't only asking about market size or how fast we could ship a product. They wanted to know how we think about the data problem in formal math, how autoformalization connects to proving, and what it means to build a system that can conjecture and prove, not just pattern-match. That told me they were thinking long-term.

The second thing is that they've been close to the AI ecosystem, including the frontier model side, so they understand the infrastructure and compute realities. For a research-heavy company like ours, having partners who get that you sometimes have to invest a long time in fundamentals before the big payoff is really important.

And on a personal level, as a young founder, I wanted people who would be honest with me, push back when I needed it, and also trust the team to make bold bets. That combination of conviction and candor is what made it feel like a good fit.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it came down to a few things. First, the people. When we were raising, I talked to a lot of firms, and what stood out about Menlo was that they had actually done the work. They understood what we were trying to do with Axiom, which is not a typical software company—we're trying to build an AI that can do real mathematics, discover and prove theorems, and eventually push the frontier of math forward. That's a long, research-heavy bet, and a lot of investors nod along but don't really get why it matters or how hard it is. Menlo had already been thinking seriously about where AI reasoning was going, and they asked the right questions.

Second, they had a track record with ambitious AI companies. They'd backed Anthropic early, and they'd set aside real capital specifically for AI, so they weren't just following the hype. They understood that the timelines in this space can be unusual—you might have long stretches where the progress is happening inside the research and not showing up as a flashy product yet. I wanted partners who were comfortable with that.

And third, there was just alignment on how to build. I came out of academia—I was doing math at MIT and then Stanford, and I'd spent years around mathematicians. I care a lot about rigor and about doing this properly, not shipping something that looks impressive but is hollow underneath. Menlo seemed to respect that. They weren't pushing us to turn into a chatbot wrapper or chase quick revenue. They understood that if we actually succeed at what we're trying to do, the value is enormous and it compounds, so the right move is to give the team the room to do serious work.

So it wasn't really a decision about a term sheet. It was about who I wanted in the room for the next ten years, especially on the hard days. And Menlo felt like the kind of partner who would still be excited about the mission then.
